chapters.title: What a Gaussian splat is (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
A Gaussian splat is a way of storing a three dimensional scene so that photographs of it can be reproduced from any viewpoint. The scene is a set of small soft ellipsoids called 3D Gaussians. Each Gaussian is defined by eleven numbers plus a colour description: a position in space, three axis lengths that give its size along each axis, a rotation that orients those axes, an opacity between zero and one, and a set of spherical harmonic coefficients that describe its colour and how that colour changes with the direction it is seen from.

The word Gaussian refers to the shape of the density. The influence of one primitive falls off from its centre following the bell curve of the normal distribution, extended to three dimensions, so a primitive has no hard edge. Its covariance matrix, built from the axis lengths and the rotation, decides how stretched and how tilted the bell is. A long thin Gaussian can lie along a wire; a flat one can lie in a wall; a round one can fill a blob of foliage.

A scene is typically between one hundred thousand and a few million of these primitives. They are not connected to each other, they have no surface, and nothing says where an object begins or ends. The only thing that matters is that, when the whole set is rendered from the positions of the original cameras, the images match the photographs.

chapters.title: What a Gaussian splat is (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
Rendering is the key operation. To draw one view, each Gaussian is projected onto the image plane, where it becomes a two dimensional ellipse with its own soft falloff. The ellipses are sorted from nearest to farthest, and every pixel composites them in that order the way layers of tinted glass combine: each layer contributes its colour weighted by its opacity and by how much light has survived the layers in front of it. This is the same alpha compositing that volume rendering and neural radiance fields use, but applied to a sorted list of primitives instead of samples along a ray, which is why it runs in real time on a GPU.

The rendering is differentiable. Every step from the parameters of a Gaussian to the colour of a pixel is a smooth function, or close enough to one, so the derivative of a loss between the rendered image and the photograph can be traced back to every parameter. That is what makes the representation trainable by gradient descent, and the whole method rests on it.

Against photogrammetry meshes, splats win on anything fuzzy, thin or translucent, and on view dependent shading, and they look like photographs. Against neural radiance fields, they train in minutes on a GPU rather than hours and render at interactive rates. The cost is that a splat is appearance only. It has no geometry a game engine or a physics system can use, it cannot be relit, and the lighting of the capture day is baked into it.

chapters.title: The pipeline end to end (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
The pipeline that splatrs implements has six stages, and the first one is not in the tool at all.

Stage one is capture: photographing or filming the scene so that every surface is seen sharply from many overlapping viewpoints under constant exposure and constant light. Most failures of the final result trace back to this stage.

Stage two is structure from motion, done by COLMAP. It finds feature points in every image, matches them across images, works out where each camera was and how it was oriented, and triangulates a sparse cloud of three dimensional points with colours. It also calibrates the camera and, in a final step called undistortion, resamples the images into ideal pinhole images so that the renderer does not have to model lens distortion.

Stage three is initialisation. Every sparse point becomes one Gaussian: its position is the point, its colour is the point colour stored in the zero order harmonic, its size comes from the distance to its three nearest neighbours, its rotation is the identity, and its opacity starts at one tenth.

Stage four is optimisation. Thirty thousand times, one photograph is chosen at random, the scene is rendered from that photograph's camera, the rendered image is compared with the photograph using a loss that mixes an absolute difference term with a structural similarity term, the gradient of that loss with respect to every parameter of every Gaussian is computed by the backward passes, and the Adam optimiser nudges all the parameters.

chapters.title: The pipeline end to end (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
Stage five, interleaved with four during the first half of training, is adaptive density control. Every hundred iterations, Gaussians whose positions keep receiving large gradients are duplicated if small or split in two if large, Gaussians that have become nearly transparent are deleted, and every three thousand iterations all opacities are reset to a low value so that the optimiser can reconsider which ones deserve to exist.

Stage six is export. The parameters are written to a PLY file in the layout the original implementation defined, which has become the common format of the whole ecosystem, and that file goes into Blender, a web viewer or a game engine.

The following chapters go through each stage in the order the data flows, with the conventions and formulas splatrs uses, and then cover how the implementation was checked, how fast it is, and where the research has gone since the original paper.

chapters.title: Capturing: camera, settings and formats (1 of 3)
chapters.text:
Capture is the stage that decides the ceiling of the result, and it has to be right before anything else matters. The method needs a static scene under constant light, seen sharply from many overlapping positions, with every image taken by the same camera at the same settings.

Any camera with manual control works, including a phone in a manual or professional mode. A mirrorless or SLR camera with a prime lens gives the cleanest images. A phone in its default mode is the worst choice, because its computational photography merges several frames and applies a different tone curve to every shot, so the same surface is a different colour in different images.

Use one camera and one lens for the whole capture and never touch the zoom. That lets COLMAP share a single calibration across all images, which makes registration far more robust. A moderate wide angle, around twenty four to thirty five millimetres full frame equivalent, gives generous overlap and little distortion. Fisheye lenses can be used with the appropriate COLMAP model and undistortion, but they spend pixels on distorted corners.

chapters.title: Capturing: camera, settings and formats (2 of 3)
chapters.text:
Set everything to manual and lock it. Focus once at a distance that keeps the subject sharp and switch to manual focus. Choose an aperture around f/5.6 to f/8 for depth of field; a blurred background is a defect here. Set the shutter to one two hundred fiftieth of a second or faster when hand held, and raise ISO as far as that requires, because noise is far less harmful than motion blur: blur destroys the features structure from motion needs and smears every edge the splat learns. Fix white balance to a preset. Fix exposure and leave it fixed when the camera turns towards a window; a clipped highlight is better than inconsistent exposure across the set. Disable HDR, night and smart modes, electronic stabilization, and any automatic per shot adjustment. Shoot in constant light, on an overcast day or indoors with all lights on and the sun not moving across the scene, and finish in one session.

Shoot RAW when the camera offers it and convert every file with identical settings to eight bit JPEG at quality ninety five or higher, or to PNG. splatrs and COLMAP read JPEG and PNG, and the loss expects eight bit sRGB. Keep every image at the same resolution and orientation, do not crop or rotate individual frames, and keep the originals. Twelve to twenty four megapixels is plenty; training downsamples, while COLMAP extracts features at full resolution.

chapters.title: Capturing: camera, settings and formats (3 of 3)
chapters.text: Video is acceptable when stills are impractical, with the same rules: highest resolution and bitrate, manual shutter at one two hundred fiftieth or faster regardless of cinematic convention, locked exposure, focus and white balance, stabilization off, slow movement. Frames are extracted at two to four per second with ffmpeg and treated as an unordered set of photographs; consecutive near identical frames add compute and no information, and rolling shutter skews fast pans in a way the pinhole model cannot describe. Frames from video are softer and noisier than stills from the same sensor.

chapters.title: Capturing: moving the camera (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
The goal of camera movement is that every surface is seen sharply from many directions, each photograph overlaps its neighbours by about two thirds, and the camera position changes between shots. Rotating in place produces a panorama with no parallax, from which structure from motion can recover no depth at all. The camera must translate.

For an object or a small subject, walk at least three complete orbits at different heights, below, level and above, taking a photograph every ten to fifteen degrees, which is twenty four to thirty six per orbit, then add close ups of detailed areas and a few views from above. One hundred to two hundred photographs is typical. Keep the background static. A turntable with a fixed camera does not work, because the background then disagrees with the object from shot to shot; it only works with a featureless masked background, which this tool does not support.

For a room, walk slowly along the walls and through the middle, photographing both outward and inward at two heights, so that every wall, the floor and the ceiling appear in several images from different positions. Doorways and corners need extra coverage because they are where chains of registration break. Two hundred to five hundred photographs is typical, and a dense run of photographs through each doorway links adjacent rooms.

For a building or an outdoor space, walk several loops at different distances and photograph each facade from many angles including oblique ones. Sky will not reconstruct and appears as a faint shell; far background gets few consistent observations and produces floaters, which more images at more distances reduce.

Avoid pure forward motion along a corridor without side views, avoid long runs of nearly identical frames, and avoid gaps where two parts of the scene share no photographs.

chapters.title: Capturing: moving the camera (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
Scenes that resist the technique: anything that moves during the capture, including people, pets, foliage in wind, water, clouds and sun shadows; glossy and mirror surfaces, which get reconstructed as phantom objects behind the surface, and transparent objects, which become partial fog, though a polarising filter helps with glass and water; textureless surfaces, which give structure from motion nothing to match, and which temporary markers can fix when acceptable; and thin structures, which need many close views.

No stabilization, ordering or prior registration is required. Structure from motion registers unordered stills on its own, and in camera electronic stabilization is harmful because it crops and warps each frame differently. A gimbal only reduces motion blur. The result has arbitrary scale and no up direction, both of which are set by hand when the splat is imported into a modelling tool.

chapters.title: Cameras and coordinates (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
Every stage depends on a precise agreement about cameras, and splatrs uses COLMAP's conventions throughout because its input comes from COLMAP.

A pinhole camera is described by four intrinsic numbers and a pose. The intrinsics are the focal lengths in pixels along x and y, usually equal, and the principal point, which is where the optical axis meets the image. The pose is a rotation and a translation that take a point from world coordinates to camera coordinates: multiply by the rotation matrix, then add the translation. In camera coordinates the camera looks down the positive z axis, x points right and y points down. A point at depth z projects to the pixel coordinate focal length times x over z plus the principal point, and likewise for y.

Pixel coordinates are continuous, and the pixel with integer index i has its centre at i plus one half. COLMAP writes principal points in this convention, and the rasterizer evaluates each Gaussian at pixel centres, so the two agree without any half pixel fudge.

The reference implementation ignores the principal point and assumes it sits at the image centre. splatrs uses the recorded value. After undistortion COLMAP's principal point is usually a few pixels off centre, and honouring it costs nothing.

COLMAP stores the rotation as a quaternion in the order w, x, y, z, with w the scalar part. The camera centre in world coordinates is minus the transpose of the rotation times the translation, which is used for the direction from which each Gaussian is viewed when its colour is evaluated.

chapters.title: Cameras and coordinates (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
Lens distortion matters because the renderer models an ideal pinhole. COLMAP estimates distortion during structure from motion with models such as SIMPLE_RADIAL or OPENCV, and its image undistorter then resamples every image so that straight lines are straight and writes a new model with PINHOLE cameras. splatrs refuses any other camera model and prints the undistortion command, because training on distorted images against a pinhole model fits the lens into the geometry as a systematic error.

The scene extent, a single number used to scale the position learning rate and the densification thresholds, follows the reference: compute the mean of the camera centres, take the largest distance of any centre from that mean, and multiply by one point one. It is computed over the training cameras only, after any evaluation hold out.

Downscaling, which the trainer does to make CPU training practical, resamples the images with a Lanczos filter and scales the focal lengths and principal point by the exact ratio of new to old size, so integer rounding of the size never introduces a geometric error.

chapters.title: Structure from motion (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
Structure from motion is the stage that turns an unordered pile of photographs into calibrated cameras, poses and a sparse point cloud. splatrs delegates it to COLMAP, which is the standard choice, and understanding what COLMAP does explains most of the capture rules.

Feature extraction finds a few thousand distinctive points in each image using SIFT, the scale invariant feature transform. Each point gets a descriptor, a vector that summarises the image gradient pattern around it in a way that survives changes of scale, rotation and moderate changes of viewpoint and brightness. Textureless surfaces yield no features, which is why bare walls and clear sky are invisible to this stage.

Matching compares descriptors between pairs of images and keeps pairs of points that look alike. Exhaustive matching tries every pair of images and is reliable but quadratic in the number of images. Sequential matching assumes the images were taken in order and compares each with its neighbours, with loop detection for revisits. Vocabulary tree matching uses a trained index to find likely partners and scales to tens of thousands of images.

The incremental mapper starts from one well connected image pair, estimates their relative pose from the matches, triangulates the matched points, and then registers one more image at a time by finding where it must be to see the already triangulated points. Every few images it runs bundle adjustment, a nonlinear least squares problem that adjusts all camera parameters and all point positions together to minimise reprojection error, the distance between where each point projects and where it was observed. The result is accurate to a fraction of a pixel when the images are sharp and overlap well.

chapters.title: Structure from motion (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
Two properties follow from this. First, nothing has to be ordered, stabilised or registered beforehand. The images are treated as a set; registration is the output, not the input. Video is accepted only as a source of still frames. Second, the reconstruction is defined up to an unknown global scale and an arbitrary choice of origin and orientation. A splat therefore has no metric units and no notion of up, which is why a result usually has to be rotated and scaled when it is imported into Blender.

Electronic stabilization in a camera breaks the assumption that all frames share one calibration, because it crops and warps each frame differently, so it must be off. Motion blur destroys the features, so a fast shutter matters more than low noise. Changing exposure changes descriptors slightly and, more importantly, gives the later optimisation inconsistent colours to fit.

Methods that skip this stage exist. COLMAP-free 3DGS and Nope-NeRF grow the scene frame by frame from video while estimating poses. DUSt3R, MASt3R, VGGT and MapAnything are networks that predict dense geometry and cameras directly from image sets and handle texture-poor and sparse-view cases that defeat SIFT. Their poses are less precise than bundle adjustment, and the strongest current results still use them, if at all, as an initialisation for COLMAP.

chapters.title: Parameters and spherical harmonics (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
How the parameters of a Gaussian are stored decides what the optimiser can and cannot break, and splatrs stores them exactly as the reference implementation does, in unconstrained form.

Axis lengths are stored as natural logarithms and exponentiated before use, so a scale can never become zero or negative no matter what step the optimiser takes. Opacity is stored as a logit and passed through the logistic sigmoid, so it always lands strictly between zero and one. The rotation is stored as four quaternion components that are not kept normalised; they are normalised every time they are used, so any four numbers describe a valid rotation. This is the type-driven idea of making invalid states unrepresentable, applied to a numerical optimiser: the search space has no illegal points.

The position is stored directly as three world coordinates. The colour is stored as spherical harmonic coefficients, sixteen per colour channel for degree three, forty eight numbers in all.

Spherical harmonics are a basis of functions on the sphere, the analogue of a Fourier series for directions. Degree zero is a constant, which gives a view independent colour. Degree one adds three functions that vary linearly with the direction components, which lets a surface be brighter from one side. Degrees two and three add five and seven functions with faster variation, which capture sheen, soft highlights and the way foliage changes brightness as the viewing angle changes. The colour seen from a direction is the sum of each coefficient times its basis function evaluated at that direction, plus one half, clamped at zero.

chapters.title: Parameters and spherical harmonics (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
The direction used is the unit vector from the camera centre to the Gaussian's position. It changes with the position, so the colour gradient also flows into the position through the derivative of the basis functions with respect to direction, and through the derivative of normalisation. splatrs includes that path, as the reference does.

The basis constants and the ordering of the coefficients follow the reference exactly, because the exported PLY file stores the coefficients and every viewer assumes that ordering. The degree zero constant is one over two root pi, and an RGB colour c is initialised into the zero order coefficient as c minus one half divided by that constant, which is the inverse of the evaluation formula.

Training raises the active degree by one every thousand iterations, starting at zero. Low frequency colour is fitted first and view dependence is added once positions and shapes have settled, which keeps the higher coefficients from absorbing errors that belong to geometry. Coefficients of inactive degrees receive zero gradient and stay at their initial zero.

chapters.title: Projection (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
Projection takes one Gaussian and one camera and produces everything the rasterizer needs: a two dimensional centre, a two dimensional shape, a depth, a radius, an opacity and a colour. It follows the elliptical weighted average splatting of Zwicker and colleagues from 2001, as the 3D Gaussian splatting paper adopted it.

The position is transformed into camera coordinates. If its depth is at or below the near plane, two tenths of a unit by default as in the reference, the Gaussian is culled for this view.

The three dimensional covariance is built as the rotation matrix of the normalised quaternion times the diagonal matrix of the axis lengths, and that product times its own transpose. This is always symmetric and positive semidefinite by construction.

Perspective projection is not linear, so it is replaced by its best linear approximation at the Gaussian's centre, the Jacobian. The Jacobian is a two by three matrix whose entries are the focal length over depth on the diagonal and minus the focal length times the lateral coordinate over depth squared in the last column. The two dimensional covariance is then the Jacobian times the camera rotation times the three dimensional covariance times the transposes of both, a two by two matrix.

The Jacobian is evaluated at a point clamped to a frustum enlarged by thirty percent on each side. Without the clamp a Gaussian far outside the view, where the approximation is poor, can produce a huge ellipse and numerical trouble. splatrs uses the clamp limits from gsplat, which are asymmetric and account for the principal point.

chapters.title: Projection (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
A small constant, three tenths of a pixel squared, is added to both diagonal entries of the two dimensional covariance. This dilation guarantees every Gaussian covers at least a few pixels, which keeps gradients flowing to tiny ones, and acts as a crude low pass filter. The reference adds it silently. Mip-Splatting observed that the dilation brightens small Gaussians, because a wider ellipse with the same opacity deposits more light, and corrected it by multiplying the opacity by the square root of the ratio of the determinant before dilation to the determinant after. splatrs offers that correction as the antialias option.

The conic is the inverse of the dilated covariance, three numbers A, B and C such that the exponent at a pixel offset is minus one half of A times dx squared plus two B times dx dy plus C times dy squared. The radius is the ceiling of three times the square root of the larger eigenvalue of the dilated covariance, a conservative three sigma extent, and from it the rectangle of sixteen pixel tiles the Gaussian may touch is computed and clamped to the image. A Gaussian whose rectangle is empty is culled.

The two dimensional centre uses the unclamped coordinates, the depth is the camera space z, and the effective opacity is the sigmoid of the stored logit times the antialiasing compensation when enabled, otherwise times one.

chapters.title: Rasterization (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
Rasterization composites the projected Gaussians into an image. The reference implementation organises it around sixteen by sixteen pixel tiles so that thousands of GPU threads can work independently, and splatrs keeps the same organisation because it is also a good fit for CPU cores and because it defines exactly which Gaussians touch which pixels.

Binning first. Every visible Gaussian is added to the list of every tile in its rectangle, one entry per tile. The entries are generated in Gaussian order so that each Gaussian's entries sit next to each other, and a sort key is built for each entry from the tile index in the high bits and the bit pattern of the depth, as a 32 bit float, in the low bits. Positive floats sort correctly when compared as integers, so sorting the keys groups entries by tile and orders each tile's entries from near to far. A final scan records where each tile's run starts and ends. The sort is deterministic because ties are broken by entry index.

chapters.title: Rasterization (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
Compositing per pixel. The transmittance starts at one. For each entry in the tile's list in order, the exponent is evaluated at the pixel centre; if it is negative, which cannot happen for a positive definite conic but is checked for safety, the entry is skipped. Alpha is the opacity times the exponential of minus the exponent, clamped at ninety nine hundredths so no single Gaussian is fully opaque. Entries with alpha below one over two hundred fifty five are skipped as invisible. If the transmittance after this entry would fall below one ten thousandth the pixel is finished and the remaining entries are ignored. Otherwise the colour accumulates alpha times transmittance times the entry colour, the transmittance is multiplied by one minus alpha, and the entry's index is recorded as the last contributor. At the end the background colour is added weighted by the remaining transmittance, and the final transmittance and the last contributor index are kept for the backward pass.

splatrs arranges the loops with entries outermost and pixels innermost. Each entry computes, once per tile, the bounding rectangle of pixels where its alpha can reach the threshold, derived from the conic and the opacity, and visits only those pixels while per pixel state carries the compositing. The result is identical to a per pixel walk over the whole list, and a test compares the two on a random scene, but the work drops from every entry times every pixel of the tile to roughly the true footprint of each splat. It also skips the exponential for pixels that cannot pass the threshold.

Floating point summation order is fixed, so a render is bitwise reproducible from run to run.

chapters.title: The loss and its gradient (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
The loss compares the rendered image with the photograph. The reference uses a weighted sum: eight tenths of the mean absolute difference, L1, plus two tenths of one minus the structural similarity index, SSIM, and splatrs uses the same.

L1 on its own fits colours but tolerates blur, because a slightly blurred image has a small absolute error. SSIM measures local structure: it compares means, variances and covariance of the two images inside an eleven by eleven Gaussian window with standard deviation one and a half, and it penalises lost contrast and lost detail even where the average colour is right. The combination fits both colour and sharpness.

SSIM at a pixel is a ratio. The numerator is two times the product of the local means plus a small constant, times two times the local covariance plus another constant. The denominator is the sum of the squared means plus the first constant, times the sum of the variances plus the second. The constants are one hundredth squared and three hundredths squared and keep the ratio stable where the image is flat. The windowed statistics are computed by a separable Gaussian blur with zero padding, so the output has the same size as the input, as in the reference's PyTorch version. Each blur is parallel over image rows.

chapters.title: The loss and its gradient (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
The gradient of mean SSIM with respect to the rendered image uses a property of the blur: because the window is symmetric, the blur is its own adjoint. The per pixel SSIM depends on the render through three blurred quantities, the mean of the render, the mean of its square, and the mean of its product with the photograph. Differentiating the ratio with respect to each of the three gives three fields; blurring those fields and combining them with the render and the photograph gives the gradient at every pixel in closed form, without automatic differentiation.

The L1 gradient is the sign of the difference divided by the number of values. The combined gradient is the weighted sum of the two.

Peak signal to noise ratio is reported for monitoring only. It is computed after clamping both images to the unit interval, as the reference metric does, and summed in double precision so that large images do not accumulate rounding error.

A note on finite difference testing of this loss: the absolute value in L1 has a kink wherever the render crosses the photograph, so central differences are unreliable right at those pixels. The L1 gradient is therefore checked on its own at random pixels, and the whole chain from parameters to loss is checked with the SSIM term alone, which is smooth.

chapters.title: Backward through the rasterizer (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
The backward pass of the rasterizer turns the gradient of the loss with respect to pixels into gradients with respect to the screen space quantities of each Gaussian: its two dimensional centre, its conic, its opacity and its colour. It walks each pixel's contributors in reverse order, exactly as the reference CUDA code does.

The forward pass kept the final transmittance and the index of the last contributing entry per pixel. The backward pass starts from that transmittance and, moving from the last contributor towards the first, divides by one minus alpha at each contributing entry to recover the transmittance that was in front of it. This avoids storing a transmittance per pixel per Gaussian.

The gradient with respect to a Gaussian's colour is simple: alpha times the transmittance in front of it times the pixel gradient, per channel.

The gradient with respect to its alpha has three parts. Raising alpha adds more of this Gaussian's colour, weighted by the transmittance in front. It also removes light from everything behind, which is accounted for by a running quantity the reference calls accumulated record: the colour that the entries behind this one would produce if they started from full transmittance, updated by the recurrence new record equals last alpha times last colour plus one minus last alpha times old record. And it reduces the background contribution, which enters as minus the final transmittance over one minus alpha times the dot product of background colour and pixel gradient.

chapters.title: Backward through the rasterizer (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
Alpha equals opacity times the Gaussian value unless it was clamped at ninety nine hundredths, in which case it is constant and none of the following gradients flow. Otherwise the opacity gradient is the Gaussian value times the alpha gradient, and the gradient with respect to the exponent is minus opacity times the Gaussian value times the alpha gradient. From the exponent, the chain rule gives the gradient with respect to the pixel offset, and since the offset is pixel minus centre, the centre gradient is its negative; and it gives the conic gradients as half the offset squared for A, the product of the offsets for B, and half the other offset squared for C.

splatrs reports the true gradient with respect to the three conic numbers. The reference stores half of the B gradient and doubles it later; the end result is the same.

For AbsGS densification, each entry also accumulates the absolute value of every pixel's contribution to the centre gradient, alongside the signed sum.

Per entry gradients are written into a flat array through relaxed atomic stores, each slot written by exactly one tile task, and then summed per Gaussian over that Gaussian's contiguous range of entries. No locks, no unsafe code, and a reduction order that is fixed, so gradients are reproducible.

chapters.title: Backward through the projection (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
The projection backward pass takes the four screen space gradients of one Gaussian and returns gradients with respect to its eleven geometric parameters and forty eight colour coefficients. It recomputes the forward intermediates rather than storing them, so memory per Gaussian is the parameter record itself. The derivation is a sequence of matrix calculus identities, each of which the finite difference tests exercise.

Colour first. Where a channel was clamped at zero, nothing flows. Otherwise the gradient of each coefficient is the pixel colour gradient times its basis value, and the direction gradient is the sum over coefficients of the colour gradient times the coefficient times the derivative of the basis function. The direction is the normalised vector from the camera centre to the position, so its derivative with respect to the position is the identity minus the outer product of the direction with itself, divided by the distance.

Opacity. The effective opacity is sigmoid of the logit times the compensation. The logit gradient is the effective opacity gradient times the compensation times sigmoid times one minus sigmoid.

Conic. The conic is the inverse of the dilated two dimensional covariance with entries a, b, c and determinant a c minus b squared. Differentiating the three entries of the inverse with respect to a, b and c gives nine closed form terms over the determinant squared. When antialiasing is on, the compensation is the square root of the ratio of the undilated to the dilated determinant, and its gradient adds terms to a, b and c through both determinants.

chapters.title: Backward through the projection (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
The two dimensional covariance is T times the three dimensional covariance times T transpose, where T is the Jacobian times the camera rotation. With the symmetric gradient matrix G built from the a, b, c gradients, splitting the b gradient in half across the two off diagonal entries, the gradient with respect to the three dimensional covariance is T transpose G T, and the gradient with respect to T is two G T Sigma.

T is J times W. The gradient with respect to J is the T gradient times W transpose. The entries of J depend on the camera space coordinates, and differentiating them gives gradients with respect to those coordinates, including the extra term in depth when the lateral coordinate was clamped, where the clamped value equals depth times a constant. The two dimensional centre adds its own terms. The camera space gradient is then multiplied by W transpose to give the position gradient in world space, to which the colour direction term is added.

The three dimensional covariance is M times M transpose with M equal to the rotation matrix times the diagonal of the scales. Its gradient is two times the covariance gradient times M. Splitting M gives the scale gradients, multiplied by the scales to convert to log scale, and the rotation matrix gradient, which the explicit derivative of the quaternion to matrix formula turns into a quaternion gradient, finally chained through normalisation.

chapters.title: Optimisation (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
The optimiser is Adam with the reference's settings: first moment decay nine tenths, second moment decay nine hundred ninety nine thousandths, and epsilon one times ten to the minus fifteen. Adam keeps two running averages per parameter, the mean gradient and the mean squared gradient, and takes steps proportional to the first divided by the square root of the second. The effect is that every parameter moves at roughly its own learning rate regardless of how large or small its raw gradient is, which matters here because position gradients and colour gradients differ by orders of magnitude.

Each group of parameters has its own learning rate. Positions start at one point six times ten to the minus four times the scene extent and decay exponentially to one hundredth of that over thirty thousand iterations, so Gaussians move freely early and settle later. Log scales use five thousandths, rotations one thousandth, opacity twenty five thousandths, the zero order colour twenty five ten thousandths, and the higher harmonics one twentieth of that.

In splatrs the Adam moments are stored as parameter shaped records, one for the first moment and one for the second, in vectors parallel to the parameter vector. Densification appends zero moments for new Gaussians and removes the moments of pruned ones with the same mask, so the three vectors cannot drift out of step. A single global step count drives the bias correction, which is what the reference's optimiser surgery produces as well.

One view is trained per iteration. The views are shuffled, drawn without replacement until the list is empty, and reshuffled, so every photograph is seen once per epoch.

chapters.title: Optimisation (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
The ordering within an iteration is: raise the harmonic degree if it is a multiple of a thousand, render, compute the loss, run the two backward passes, accumulate densification statistics, take the Adam step, then run density control if due. The reference runs density control before the step, but it replaces every parameter tensor when it does, which leaves the new tensors without gradients, so the reference effectively skips the step on those iterations. splatrs takes the step first, as gsplat does; this is a documented deliberate difference.

Opacity resets zero the opacity moments, as the reference does, so the optimiser does not immediately push opacities back up from stale momentum.

Learning rates and schedule are hyperparameters tuned by the reference authors on their benchmark scenes and left unchanged here.

chapters.title: Adaptive density control (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
The sparse point cloud from structure from motion has far too few points and none in textureless or thin regions, so the set of Gaussians must grow and reshape during training. The reference calls this adaptive density control.

The signal is the gradient of the loss with respect to each Gaussian's two dimensional centre, accumulated across iterations. A Gaussian that keeps wanting to move in screen space is one that is trying to cover a region it cannot: either it is too small and there should be more of them, or it is too large and should be split. splatrs converts the pixel space gradient to the normalised device coordinate space the reference uses by multiplying by half the image size, so the reference threshold of two ten thousandths applies unchanged. The statistic is the mean of the gradient norm over the iterations in which the Gaussian was visible.

Every hundred iterations between iteration five hundred and fifteen thousand, Gaussians above the threshold are processed. If the largest axis is at most one percent of the scene extent, the Gaussian is cloned: an identical copy is added, and the two will drift apart under their own gradients. If larger, it is split into two children sampled from its own distribution, with the same rotation, colour and opacity, axes divided by one point six, and the parent removed.

chapters.title: Adaptive density control (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
Pruning follows. Gaussians whose opacity is below five thousandths are deleted; after the first opacity reset, so are those whose largest axis exceeds ten percent of the scene extent, which are usually floaters covering sky or background. The reference also computes a largest screen radius per Gaussian for pruning, but it zeroes that array before it tests it, so the test never fires; gsplat's default strategy leaves the equivalent disabled. splatrs makes it an explicit option that is off by default.

Every three thousand iterations all opacities are clamped to at most one hundredth. This sounds destructive, and it is deliberate: Gaussians that are needed quickly regain opacity, floaters and duplicates do not and get pruned at the next step. After every densification step the statistics are reset.

AbsGS, by Ye and colleagues in 2024, noticed that gradients from different pixels can cancel when they pull in opposite directions, hiding a Gaussian that should be split. It accumulates absolute per pixel contributions instead. splatrs implements it as the absgrad option, with the paper's threshold of eight ten thousandths.

3DGS-MCMC, by Kheradmand and colleagues in 2024, replaces the whole heuristic with a view of training as sampling: Gaussians are relocated rather than cloned, noise is added to positions, and a regulariser controls the count under a fixed budget. It is more predictable about memory and is on the roadmap.

chapters.title: Verification (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
The implementation was written to be checked rather than trusted, and the checks are part of the test suite.

The central tool is the scalar type. The crate defines one type alias that is 32 bit float by default and 64 bit under a cargo feature, and all geometry, parameters, gradients and images use it. The same code therefore runs at double precision, where central finite differences resolve gradients to about one part in a hundred thousand, which is tight enough to catch a wrong sign, a missing factor of two, a transposed matrix or a dropped term.

Each backward pass is tested in isolation. The spherical harmonic basis derivatives are compared with finite differences of the basis. The projection backward pass is tested through a random linear functional of its outputs for all fifty nine parameters of random Gaussians, with and without antialiasing, at every harmonic degree, and in a configuration where the Jacobian clamp is active. The rasterizer backward pass is tested on nine overlapping screen space Gaussians over a forty by twenty eight image, for every centre, conic, opacity and colour entry. The SSIM gradient and the full photometric loss gradient are tested at random pixels. Finally the whole chain from parameters through projection, rasterization and the smooth part of the loss is tested for six overlapping Gaussians, which guards the composition of the pieces.

The tiled rasterizer with its entry outer loops and per entry pixel rectangles is compared against a plain per pixel compositor with no acceleration structure on a random scene with large, small and nearly transparent Gaussians; the two agree to floating point noise.

chapters.title: Verification (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
Two synthetic training tests render a random ground truth scene with the renderer itself and then fit it from a perturbed initialisation, once with densification off and once with the full schedule compressed into five hundred iterations, and assert a large PSNR improvement. A command line test runs info, train and render on a generated project.

The COLMAP binary reader was run on files written by COLMAP's own Python reference script, including non-empty observation lists and point tracks, and the scene extent it computed matched the value computed in Python to every printed digit. The camera model table was checked against COLMAP's C++ header, which defines the newest fisheye model as number eleven with sixteen parameters. The PLY layout was checked against the reference save and load functions, including the channel major ordering of the higher harmonic coefficients.

An independent review by a second agent that had not seen the code being written went through the mathematics against the reference Python sources and found no defects in the core; it found seven peripheral issues, in the evaluation split, a degenerate input to the nearest neighbour tree, metric precision, output naming and thresholds, all of which were fixed.

Clippy passes with warnings denied in both precisions, and the crate forbids unsafe code.

chapters.title: Output and the ecosystem (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
A trained scene is written as a PLY file in the layout the reference implementation defined in its save function, and that layout has become the lingua franca of the field.

PLY is a simple container: a text header that lists the properties of each vertex, followed by binary little endian records. Each Gaussian is one vertex with position x, y, z; three normal components that are always zero and kept only for compatibility; three zero order colour coefficients; the higher order coefficients, forty five of them for degree three, stored channel major so that the fifteen coefficients of red come first, then green, then blue; the opacity as a logit; the three log scales; and the four quaternion components in the order w, x, y, z, unnormalised. Everything is a 32 bit float. splatrs reads the file back by property name, so files from other tools load as long as they use these names and float properties, and the number of higher order coefficients tells it the degree.

Blender 5.3, with its final release expected in November 2026, imports this file natively as a new point cloud type for Gaussian splats, exposes it to Geometry Nodes, and renders it in Workbench, EEVEE and Cycles. Earlier Blender versions use add-ons such as KIRI Engine's 3DGS Render or BlendSplat that read the same file. SuperSplat in the browser, PlayCanvas, Nerfstudio's viewer, Unity and Unreal plug-ins, and most phone viewers read it too.

The file is in COLMAP's world frame, whose orientation and scale are whatever structure from motion happened to pick. Blender is z up with x right and y into the screen, so an imported splat usually needs a rotation of roughly minus ninety degrees around x as a starting point, a visual levelling, and a scale.

chapters.title: Output and the ecosystem (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
For delivery over the web the file is too large: a million Gaussians at degree three is about two hundred fifty megabytes. SPZ from Niantic and SOG from PlayCanvas quantise the attributes and reduce that by five to ten times with little visible loss, and the Khronos group is standardising a glTF extension for splats. Blender 5.3 also reads SPZ. splatrs does not write these yet.

A splat in Blender behaves as a baked photograph of light. It is not affected by lights in the scene, does not cast real shadows, and does not light the objects placed inside it. Add-ons and research projects approximate relighting from estimated normals, and the inverse rendering variants of the method attempt it properly, but neither is production ready. Compositing works when the splat is the environment or the hero object and the inserted objects are lit to match the capture.

chapters.title: Performance and the CPU (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
The reference implementation and almost every successor run on CUDA, and the arithmetic explains why. The dominant cost is evaluating Gaussians at pixels. Every pixel of every image composites tens of Gaussians, a one megapixel view with twenty contributing Gaussians per pixel is twenty million evaluations, and each evaluation is an exponential and a few dozen floating point operations in the forward pass and about twice that in the backward pass. A GPU runs thousands of those in parallel.

splatrs runs this on CPU cores with rayon, in parallel over tiles for rasterization, over Gaussians for projection and its backward pass, and over image rows for the loss. The measured cost on this implementation is about fifteen nanoseconds per Gaussian pixel pair per core forward and twenty five backward, so the one megapixel view above costs close to a core second per iteration. Thirty thousand iterations on eight cores is an hour at that resolution and several hours at the resolution of a modern camera. The profile example in the repository prints the time of each phase for one iteration of a given scene.

Two optimisations keep that number from being worse. The entry outer loop with per entry pixel rectangles means each Gaussian visits only the pixels its ellipse can reach, instead of all two hundred fifty six pixels of every tile it overlaps, and the threshold on the exponent skips the exponential for pixels where the opacity cannot reach the visibility cut. Together they roughly halved the time of an iteration on the synthetic benchmark without changing a single output value.

chapters.title: Performance and the CPU (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
Memory is about two hundred forty bytes per Gaussian for the parameters, the same again for gradients and for each of the two Adam moments, plus forty four bytes per tile entry during an iteration, plus the images stored as 8 bit samples. A million Gaussians fit in a few gigabytes.

The next steps for speed are clear and ordered. Vectorising the inner loops with SIMD across eight pixels would give a few times. A wgpu compute backend, with the projection and rasterization kernels written once in WGSL and running on Intel, AMD and NVIDIA GPUs and on Apple silicon, would give a hundred times and more, and the CPU implementation would become the oracle that the GPU kernels are tested against, which is the main reason it exists. Brush, the existing Rust implementation on Burn and wgpu, shows that this path works and is already faster than gsplat on the same hardware.

The CPU implementation is the right tool for understanding, verification and small scenes, and the wrong tool for a production pipeline at full resolution.

chapters.title: Limitations and the research landscape (1 of 2)
chapters.text:
Gaussian splatting as implemented here has limits that come from the representation, from the pipeline, and from the specific choices of the original paper, and the research since 2023 has attacked all three.

From the representation: a splat has no surfaces, so it cannot be relit, cannot be collided with, and cannot be edited like a mesh. 2D Gaussian splatting by Huang and colleagues fits flat surfels instead of ellipsoids and extracts far better geometry. SuGaR by Guedon and Lepetit regularises Gaussians onto a surface and extracts a mesh. The inverse rendering variants decompose appearance into material and lighting with partial success.

From aliasing: the original method is trained at one resolution and shows artefacts when viewed at another. Mip-Splatting adds a 3D smoothing filter bounded by the sampling rate of the training cameras and a 2D filter in place of the fixed dilation; splatrs has the 2D opacity compensation and not yet the 3D filter.

From densification: the clone and split heuristic is sensitive to thresholds and image resolution and gives little control over the final count. AbsGS fixes gradient cancellation, 3DGS-MCMC replaces the heuristic with relocation under a budget, and Taming 3DGS schedules the growth to a target count. Only AbsGS is in splatrs today.

From the camera model: the method assumes pinhole cameras and global shutter. 3DGUT replaces the linearised projection with an unscented transform, which handles fisheye lenses and rolling shutter directly, without undistortion.

chapters.title: Limitations and the research landscape (2 of 2)
chapters.text:
From the capture: everything assumes a static scene and constant lighting. The 4D variants add time to each Gaussian and need synchronised multi camera rigs. Appearance embeddings and per image exposure compensation, which the 2024 update of the reference added, absorb exposure drift across a capture; splatrs does not have them yet, which is why its capture rules insist on locked exposure. Depth supervision from LiDAR or from monocular depth networks helps texture-poor and sparse-view captures, and masks exclude moving objects and the capturer's own shadow.

From structure from motion: SIFT based registration fails on texture-poor scenes and sparse views, and the learned alternatives, DUSt3R, MASt3R, VGGT and MapAnything, are closing that gap and may eventually replace the first stage altogether.

From scale: the result has no metric units and no gravity direction, which matters for anything that is measured or placed in a world.

What the method does exceptionally well remains what the original paper demonstrated: given a careful capture of a static scene, it produces a photorealistic, freely navigable reconstruction with real time rendering, and its training procedure is simple enough to implement from scratch and verify to the last derivative, which is what splatrs set out to do.
